SECURITY GUARD / PROPRIETARY SECURITY OFFICER REGISTRATION (BSIS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS SECURITY GUARD REGISTRATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California law requiring a person who will work as a security guard, security patrolperson, or in-house ("proprietary") security officer to register with the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services (BSIS), a bureau of the Department of Consumer Affairs, before performing those duties, and requiring the business that employs that person to itself be licensed or registered with BSIS. It states facts drawn from the Private Security Services Act and the Proprietary Security Services Act (Business and Professions Code Division 3, Chapter 11.5 and Chapter 11.4) about who must register, the background-check and training steps that precede registration, and the employer's duty to confirm that registration is current. Acme, Inc. is considering Jordan T. Reyes for the position of Security Guard. This document does not determine whether that specific position falls within a statutory registration requirement, whether any exemption applies, or whether Jordan T. Reyes has in fact been registered by BSIS; it also does not address the separate general Live Scan / DOJ fingerprint background-check framework (Penal Code Section 11105.3) covered in another information sheet in this corpus, or the Farm Labor Contractor, Talent Agency, or Public Works Contractor registration schemes covered elsewhere in this corpus, none of which govern security guard or proprietary security officer registration.

TWO STATUTORY CATEGORIES: CONTRACT SECURITY GUARDS AND PROPRIETARY (IN-HOUSE) SECURITY OFFICERS
California regulates security personnel who work for a licensed private patrol operator (a contract security guard business) under the Private Security Services Act, and separately regulates unarmed security personnel who work exclusively for a single, non-security employer under the Proprietary Security Services Act. Business and Professions Code Section 7574.01 defines a "proprietary private security employer" as a person with employees who provide security services only for that employer, and defines a "proprietary private security officer" as an unarmed individual employed exclusively by one employer whose primary duty is to provide security services for that employer, whose services are not contracted to any other entity, who is required to wear a distinctive uniform identifying the individual as a security officer, and who is likely to interact with the public while performing those duties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Proprietary private security employer” means a person who has one or more employees who provide security services for the employer and only for the employer."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.01(f) (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, definition of "proprietary private security employer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.01.)
  "“Proprietary private security officer” means an unarmed individual who is employed exclusively by any one employer whose primary duty is to provide security services for their employer, whose services are not contracted to any other entity or person, and who is not exempt pursuant to Section 7582.2, and who meets both of the following criteria:(1) Is required to wear a distinctive uniform clearly identifying the individual as a security officer.(2) Is likely to interact with the public while performing their duties."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.01(g) (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, definition of "proprietary private security officer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.01.)
  Known gap: Chapter 11.4 defines "proprietary private security officer" as an unarmed individual only; an in-house employee who carries a firearm or other deadly weapon while providing security services for a single employer falls outside that definition and is instead subject to the separate Private Patrol Operator / armed-guard and firearms-permit provisions of Chapter 11.5, which this document addresses only insofar as those provisions independently apply to contract security guards and does not analyze for an armed in-house context.

A PROPRIETARY PRIVATE SECURITY EMPLOYER MUST ITSELF BE REGISTERED WITH BSIS
Before an employer who is not otherwise a licensed private patrol operator uses its own unarmed, uniformed employees to provide security services solely for itself, Business and Professions Code Section 7574.12 requires that employer to register with the Department of Consumer Affairs as a proprietary private security employer, unless a specific statutory exemption applies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No person shall engage in the business of a proprietary private security employer unless registered with the department pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.12 (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, registration required to engage in business as a proprietary private security employer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.12.)
  Known gap: Section 7574.12 requires registration of the employer itself; it does not, by its own text, also state the separate requirement that each individual proprietary private security officer working for that employer be individually registered, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This clause also does not resolve, for a specific employer, whether that employer's use of security personnel meets the statutory definition of "proprietary private security employer" in the first place.

APPLICATION, FINGERPRINT-BASED BACKGROUND CHECK, AND TWO-YEAR CARD FOR A PROPRIETARY SECURITY OFFICER
An individual seeking registration as a proprietary private security officer applies to the Department of Consumer Affairs and, under Business and Professions Code Section 7574.11, must submit fingerprints that the department forwards to the Department of Justice for a state and federal criminal history check, along with a statutory application fee. Upon approval, the chief of the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services issues the applicant a registration card that is valid for two years from the date of issue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The department shall submit to the Department of Justice fingerprint images and related information required by the Department of Justice for all proprietary private security officer registration applicants, as defined by subdivision (f) of Section 7574.01, for the purposes of obtaining information as to the existence and content of a record of state or federal convictions and state or federal arrests"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.11(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, fingerprint submission for a Department of Justice background check (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.11.)
  "Upon approval of an application for registration as a proprietary private security officer by the director, the chief shall cause to be issued to the applicant a registration card in a form approved by the director. A registration card shall be valid for two years from the date of issue."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.11(c) (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, issuance and two-year term of the registration card (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.11.)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes the application, fingerprint, and background-check requirements and the two-year card term that Section 7574.11 sets for proprietary private security officers specifically; it does not restate the separate, non-identical registration-application and fee provisions that Business and Professions Code Section 7583.9 sets for a security guard employed by a licensed private patrol operator under the different Article 4 scheme, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document, and does not report the current dollar amount of the application fee, which the statute permits to be adjusted within a stated range.

PROVISIONAL WORK AUTHORIZATION FOR A PROPRIETARY OFFICER WHILE THE REGISTRATION CARD IS PENDING
Business and Professions Code Section 7574.11(d) allows a person to begin work as a proprietary private security officer before the physical registration card arrives, provided the director has already approved the person and the person carries, while working, a hardcopy printout of the bureau's approval from the bureau's website together with either a valid California driver's license or a valid California identification card.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A person may work as a proprietary private security officer pending receipt of the registration card if he or she has been approved by the director and carries on his or her person a hardcopy printout of the bureau’s approval from the bureau’s Internet Web site and either a valid driver’s license issued pursuant to Section 12811 of the Vehicle Code or a valid identification card issued pursuant to Section 13000 of the Vehicle Code."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.11(d) (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, provisional work pending receipt of the registration card (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.11.)
  Known gap: This provisional-work provision applies by its terms to proprietary private security officers registered under Chapter 11.4. This document does not confirm whether an equivalent provision, on the same documentary terms, exists for a contract security guard employed by a private patrol operator under the separate Chapter 11.5 scheme, and does not represent that the two schemes' rules for working while an application is pending are identical.

POWER-TO-ARREST AND SKILLS TRAINING AS A CONDITION OF A CONTRACT SECURITY GUARD'S REGISTRATION
For a security guard registration issued to work for a licensed private patrol operator, Business and Professions Code Section 7583.6(a) makes completion of a course in the power to arrest and the appropriate use of force a condition for the registration to be issued in the first place. Separately, subdivision (b) requires a registrant, after the initial registration is issued, to complete at least 32 hours of security-officer-skills training within six months, with 16 of those hours completed within the first 30 days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Each applicant for a security guard registration shall complete a course in the exercise of the power to arrest and the appropriate use of force as a condition for the issuance of the registration."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), Private Security Services Act, power-to-arrest/use-of-force training as a condition of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7583.6.)
  "a security guard registrant shall complete not less than 32 hours of training in security officer skills within six months from the date an initial registration is issued. A security guard registrant shall complete 16 of the 32 hours within 30 days from the date the registration is issued."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.6(b) (California Legislative Information text), Private Security Services Act, 32-hour skills training deadline after initial registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7583.6.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 7583.6, which also contains, in subdivisions (c) through (j), additional recordkeeping duties, an annual eight-hour continuing-training requirement, who may administer the trainings, and exemptions for certain peace officers and armored vehicle guards, none of which are reproduced or analyzed in this clause.

FINGERPRINT-BASED BACKGROUND CHECK FOR A CONTRACT SECURITY GUARD'S REGISTRATION
Business and Professions Code Section 7583.9(a) requires an applicant for a security guard registration to submit an application, the registration fee, and fingerprints to the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services, which forwards the fingerprints to the Department of Justice, which in turn forwards a copy to the Federal Bureau of Investigation for purposes of a background check.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The security guard registration applicant shall submit the application, the registration fee, and their fingerprints, either in the form of classifiable fingerprint cards or in an electronic format pursuant to subdivision (c), to the bureau. The bureau shall forward the classifiable fingerprint cards to the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice shall forward one classifiable fingerprint card to the Federal Bureau of Investigation for purposes of a background check."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.9(a) (California Legislative Information text), Private Security Services Act, application, fee, and fingerprints for a security guard registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7583.9.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of Section 7583.9; the section also contains, in subdivisions (b) through (j), an allowance for the employer to advance and then withhold the application fee from the applicant's compensation, an electronic-fingerprinting alternative, and several exemptions from the fingerprint-card requirement for currently employed or reserve peace officers, none of which this clause reproduces or analyzes.

A PRIVATE PATROL OPERATOR'S DUTY TO VERIFY THAT ITS GUARDS ARE CURRENTLY REGISTERED
Business and Professions Code Section 7583.19 places an ongoing duty on a licensed private patrol operator to ascertain that each employee subject to registration is currently registered, and bars the licensee from having a person whose registration has expired or been revoked, denied, suspended, or canceled perform security guard duties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A licensee shall at all times be responsible for ascertaining that those of their employees who are subject to registration are currently registered as provided in this article. A licensee may not have a person whose registration has expired or been revoked, denied, suspended, or canceled perform security guard duties."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.19 (California Legislative Information text), Private Security Services Act, licensee's duty to verify current registration of its guards (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7583.19.)
  Known gap: Section 7583.19 states this verification duty and the bar on using an unregistered person for guard duties, but the statutory text of this section does not itself specify the disciplinary or civil consequences to the licensee for a violation; this document does not address the separate enforcement and license-discipline provisions elsewhere in the Private Security Services Act that may apply.

A STATUTORY EXEMPTION LIMITS WHO MUST REGISTER UNDER THE PROPRIETARY SECURITY SERVICES ACT
The Proprietary Security Services Act's registration requirement is not universal. Business and Professions Code Section 7574.14 lists categories of persons to whom the chapter does not apply, including an officer or employee of the United States, this state, or a political subdivision performing official duties, which the statute states covers uniformed peace officers employed part time by a public agency under a written agreement between a chief of police or sheriff and the public agency, provided the part-time employment does not exceed 50 hours in a calendar month.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An officer or employee of the United States of America, or of this state or a political subdivision thereof, while the officer or employee is engaged in the performance of their official duties, including uniformed peace officers employed part time by a public agency pursuant to a written agreement between a chief of police or sheriff and the public agency, provided the part-time employment does not exceed 50 hours in a calendar month."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.14(a) (California Legislative Information text), Proprietary Security Services Act, exemption for government officers and employees performing official duties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7574.14.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of an eight-subdivision exemption list in Section 7574.14; the remaining subdivisions (b) through (h) cover, among others, certain patrol special police officers, off-duty and retired peace officers, unarmed motion picture studio security personnel, armored contract carriers, and federally recognized tribal employers, none of which are reproduced or analyzed here. This document does not determine whether any exemption in Section 7574.14, in whole or in part, applies to a specific employer's use of a specific individual in a specific position.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding California's security guard and proprietary security officer registration requirements was reviewed by Acme, Inc. regarding Jordan T. Reyes's prospective position of Security Guard on September 1, 2026. It reflects the statutory text as of the date checked in each authority section below and does not reflect any amendments made after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

Reviewed by (on behalf of Acme, Inc.): ______________________
Date: September 1, 2026
